title: Where to Cut
the Firebreak
slides.dek: A cascade has one road through a network, its giant vulnerable component. A dozen well-chosen cuts close it; forty random ones cannot. Where you make the cut decides everything.

slides.body: On a network where each node adopts once a single neighbour does, only the *vulnerable* nodes, the ones with few enough neighbours that one is enough, can carry a spark onward. A rumour that reaches everyone, a run that empties every bank, a worm that owns every machine, is possible only when those vulnerable nodes join into one connected mass: the *giant vulnerable component*, the spine. On this fixed network of *140* nodes, *120* are vulnerable and *102* of them, 73% of the whole graph, form one spine. Break it and no single spark can go global again. So how few nodes must you pull out, and does it matter which?

It matters by *3.7x*. To contain this network, largest surviving piece under 10%, random immunization needs *44* cuts, nearly a third of the graph. Take the *hubs* first and it drops to 19. Take the *bottlenecks*, the nodes the most shortest paths run through, recomputed after every cut, and *12* will do it. The reason random loses: a vulnerable network is mostly slack. Sort every node by its traffic and the top *12 carry 43%* of it, while *38 of 120* carry essentially none. Pull a node at random and you almost certainly hit slack. Pull the busiest and the component splits. Random is a tax paid in bulk; targeting is surgery.

slides.sub: Pick a strategy, random, hubs, or bottlenecks, slide how many nodes to immunize, and watch the spine fracture live until the cascade is contained. Then see the same experiment run over 400 fresh networks, and the sorted-betweenness distribution that explains why a dozen chosen cuts beat forty blind ones. Percolation on a fixed subgraph, executed in your browser; nothing fetched, nothing remembered.
